public_rationale: The literal $2.68 rate yields $23.584 billion of training spending, so that multiplication works. But preserving the setup's $4.3 billion revenue denominator yields $13.71 billion of training spending and $18.83 billion combined. The text does not consistently specify which first-half ratio governs. Nor does the calculation establish actual second-half spending or net cash burn. A single supported or contradicted verdict would depend on choosing between those readings.
limitations: The arithmetic check uses the supplied assumptions, not independently validated financial inputs.
Annual R&D reporting does not match the claimed half-year cash-spending measure.
The roughly $0.1 billion rounding difference is not the material issue.

our_interpretation: This is a conditional extrapolation for July–December 2025, not an unqualified disclosure of actual expenditure.
The calculation treats burn as gross training plus inference spending. It does not subtract revenue and therefore is not a net-cash-burn calculation.
Two incompatible revenue denominators appear in the passage: $4.3 billion in the first-half setup and $2.5 billion in the training calculation.
Both readings must be retained because choosing one determines whether the training estimate follows.
criteria.support_condition: A consistent set of the stated first-half cost-to-revenue assumptions, applied to the assumed $8.8 billion of second-half revenue, yields approximately $23.58 billion of training spending and $28.6 billion of combined training and inference spending.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The unambiguously applicable first-half ratios yield materially different estimates, or comparable records establish that the asserted spending occurred on a materially different basis while the claimed ratio condition held.

evidence.excerpt: For $2.5bn of revenue, OpenAI spent $6.7bn in training costs — or around $2.68 per dollar of revenue. At that rate, OpenAI spent a further $23.58bn on training, bringing us to $28.6bn in burn just for the back half of 2025.

evidence.explanation: The literal $2.68 rate produces the stated training estimate. Using the $4.3 billion revenue denominator in the preceding setup produces a materially smaller estimate; this item documents the ambiguity, not actual expenditure.

evidence.explanation: The article reports $19.18 billion of R&D expense for all of 2025 from audited statements. Annual R&D expense is neither second-half training cash spending nor the result of the specified hypothetical ratios.
